26	## Traits and objects
27	
28	**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.
29	
30	**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. So where the Meet Rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads, several declarations that together cover the meet serve. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).
31	
32	**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. The checker refuses such a redeclaration where an object reaches the method of a generic self-typed trait along two paths (row 1037; `compiler.md`, "The checker's gaps", gives the form). An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier, so a program that writes one does not compile (row 650).
33	
34	**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk and the checker stop the search for a cover at the same limits, which `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", gives. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).
35	
36	**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:
37	
38	- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
39	- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.
40	
41	In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` at `X` runs. Three shapes fail when the class loads:
42	
43	- a function expression or a local function that returns `self` at `X` fails the JVM's verification (row 1050);
44	- a conditional with `self` in one arm and another value in the other fails the JVM's verification (row 1051). `StandardTotalOrder`'s `MIN` and `MAX` in the interpreter's library have this shape. So declare your own `MIN` and `MAX` in a type that extends `StandardTotalOrder` and must run compiled, as the integer types do;
45	- a body that `T` gives one of its methods, which calls a method on a value of type `X`, gives a `ClassCircularityError` where the object lists `T` first in its `extends` clause (row 1052).
46	
47	For the first two shapes, bind `self` to a variable of type `X` first, as `s: X = self`, and use `s`. For the third shape, declare the method in `T` without a body, and give the body in the object. Declaring it again in the object while `T` keeps its body still fails.
48	
49	When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. In two cases walk does not read `self` so, and its load check refuses the valid pair:
50	
51	- `T` is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
52	- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.
53	
54	**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values take a subscript, as `a[i]`: an array, for example. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile: write the bound only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library.
55	
56	Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes `Index`. A numeral at a parameter of type `Index` takes its default, a `ZZ32`, so `f(3)` is valid for `f(x: Index)`. The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Two departures:
57	
58	- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
59	- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).
60	
61	**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. Walk departs for numbers of two run-time types at one position: it refuses them, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Where the deciding elements' own comparison is `Unordered`, the answer is `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.
62	
63	**Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence, `SEQV` (P-168).** Strict equivalence is the operator `≣` (STRICTLY EQUIVALENT TO), written `SEQV` or `===` in ASCII. The operator `≡` (IDENTICAL TO, `EQV` or `EQUIV`) is a different one: logical equivalence on booleans. The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write `a <-> b`. The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:
64	
65	- values of different types are never equivalent;
66	- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
67	- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
68	- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.
69	
70	So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Two string literals of one text are one object (P-171). So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are `true`. Two string literals joined by `||` fold into one ("Numbers"), so `("a" || "b") SEQV "ab"` is `true`. A float numeral converts where `RR64` is declared ("Numbers"), so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `RR64` 0.5. The interpreter's library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false` (row 923). To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its own `≣`, declared as `===`, compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).

72	## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes
73	
74	**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: in a generic object whose `T` stayed open, a call `pick((1, 2))` of its methods `pick(x: Any)` and `pick(x: (T,T))` runs the first (row 663). Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
75	
76	- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
77	- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
78	- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
79	
80	**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
81	
82	**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
83	
84	- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
85	- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
86	
87	The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension without its condition (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
88	
89	**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
90	
91	**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call runs only under walk, also after the switch-over. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, which lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.

93	## Numbers
94	
95	**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** In the interpreter's library, seven are value objects (P-178): `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64`. `QQ` is a trait, and its values are the value object `Ratio` (P-166). Do not extend a number type in a program. Declare a program's own number type below `Number` (P-160). Such a type runs on both paths. Walk refuses an object below one of the seven at load, as `object Mine extends ZZ32`: 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'. The compiler's prelude declares no `QQ`, and still declares the other seven as traits that a type can extend (row 1003). So the checker accepts such an object, and the object dies when its class loads (row 866). The record calls this design route A, and still calls the number types "the tower", though they do not nest.
96	
97	**The team's `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` do not exist.** No library declares them. On both paths, each is undefined as a type: 'Float is undefined.' As a `typecase` arm, each takes every value, without a message (row 959). So an arm at `Int`, copied from a team test or an old note, also takes an `RR64` and a string. In their place, write `ZZ32` for `Int`, `ZZ64` for `Long`, `RR64` for `Float`, `ZZ` for `BigNum` and `NN64` for `UnsignedLong`.
98	
99	**A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** A numeral's own type is `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` with a radix point (P-174). Its static arguments are the numeral's numbers: `n` the digit count, `m` the count of digits after the point, `r` the radix, and `v` the digits read as one integer in that radix, so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. Both lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`. No numeral value exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type. The compiler's prelude follows the same design (P-37).
100	
101	A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs. Walk's message depends on the place: a top-level binding gives 'Type mismatch binding', a parameter 'got arg'. To get an infinity, overflow run-time arithmetic: for `t: RR64 = 10.0^308`, `t TIMES 10.0` is `Infinity` under walk. `x.isInfinite` tests for one. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares neither `TIMES` nor `isInfinite`.
102	
103	Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value, other than a numeral type's number, is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).
104	
105	Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). With a radix point, write `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])`. The coercion's body reads `n`, `r` and `v` as `ZZ` values without a bound, since a numeral's digits fit no fixed width (P-173, P-40). The `where` clause bounds the numerals that the type takes. 114	- on both paths, `g(5)` runs `g[\T\](x: T)` beside `g(x: NN32)`, where the rule gives `g(x: NN32)` (row 1017).
115	
116	**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
117	
118	**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types declares its own functional method `asFloat(self): RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. A numeral reaches a number type's own `=` by its coercion (P-46). So on both paths `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true` and `u =/= 0` is `false` for a zero `u: NN32`, and `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead.
119	
120	**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
121	
122	**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
123	
124	## Reductions and comprehensions
125	
126	A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
127	
128	**Where a reduction's bound names its parameter, as for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, the two paths fix an unwritten static argument from different places.** The argument is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Without it, the checker takes the reduction's expected type, and the body's type only where there is no expected type or it does not fit the reduction's bound. So `x: RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)` sums `ZZ32` elements in `RR64`, not in the body's type. A reduction whose bound does not name its parameter takes its bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types; if it is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1".
129	
130	At a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable and an assignment, the checker reads the declared type, so the two paths sum in different types (row 1008): `meth(): RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#4] huge(j)` raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk only. Write the argument there in a program for both paths. A call's argument has no expected type where the call is accepted without one. So as a call's argument, a reduction sums in its body's type on both paths. Write both arguments of `BIG MIN_MAX`, the element types of its pairs, as `BIG MIN_MAX[\ZZ32, ZZ32\][j <- 0#3] pr(j)`: the checker infers only a single static parameter (row 1007). Departures under walk:
131	
132	- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
133	- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
134	- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
135	
136	**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
137	
138	## Implementation limits
139	
140	**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). Besides a `Boolean`, walk takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition.
141	
142	**Write every parameter type.** The compiled checker refuses a parameter without a type, "Missing parameter type for", unless the exported api's declaration gives the type. Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.
143

content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.

## The caches

All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:

- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).

Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).

## The library order

The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.

Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:

- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.

Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:

    cd ProjectFortress
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s

Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.

- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.

## Name resolution

- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.

## Building

Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.

- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.

## After an edit of the library

The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.

- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.

## Symptoms of a skipped step

If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:

- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.

If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.

Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:

- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.

Two more facts help you read a run:

- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.

121	**The change.** The team's disambiguator, which walk and the compiler share, read a `typecase` arm `Id =>` whose name names no type as a binder over every value, the clause `Id: Any =>`, and let every other undefined name inside an arm's type pass without a message (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/disambiguator/TypeDisambiguator.java:240-250` and `:392-395` at 1609258002, the team's code of 2012); the team's test `compiler_tests/Compiled7.PatternMatching.b.fss:30` wrote `x => println x`. The tree now refuses such an arm on both paths with the message every undefined type name gets, 'Id is undefined.', and so a name in an arm's arrow type or static argument; an arm at a type parameter in scope tests against its static argument; a binder over every value is written `x: Any =>`; an element of a tuple of names, as `(x, y) =>`, still binds. Tests: `tests/TypecaseUndefinedArmWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/XXXTypecaseUndefinedArmCompiled.test`, `tests/TypecaseUndefinedNameInArmTypeWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/XXXTypecaseUndefinedNameInArmTypeCompiled.test`, `tests/TypecaseTypeParamArmWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/TypecaseTypeParamArmCompiled.test`, `tests/TypecaseTupleArmUndefinedNameBindsWalk.fss`. The reason: "it is a static error for a reference to a name to occur where it is not in scope in the appropriate namespace" (`Specification/basic/declarations.tex:571-572`), and the chapter's grammar makes an arm a type, `TypecaseTypes ::= ( TypeList ) | Type` (`Specification/basic/expressions/typecase.tex:69-71`); measured, an arm at `Int`, which names no type, took `2.5` on both paths and printed 'an Int'. The skill's sentence that such an arm "takes every value, without a message" no longer holds.
122	
123	**Provenance.** Row 959; the batch's fork D1, "A `typecase` arm whose name binds no type variable in scope and no declared type is refused when names are bound, on both paths", taken at its default; the tuple of names left to the curator; climb batch 33, rung D.
124	
125	### Rung V, `rung-kind-env-generic`: the kind environment of a generic declaration's types, and a `typecase` tuple pattern's names
126	
127	Revival change: none. The team's code generator crashed on, or miscompiled, programs that the team's checker passes, walk runs and the one library writes (`Library/List.fss:93-99`); after the change the compiled path does what walk does, and no source of the team's says that a clause's names are unbound or that a declaration's static parameters are out of scope in its body.
128	
129	### Rung Q, `rung-self-arm-closure`: `self` at a conditional's arm, a closure's result and a default body
130	
131	**The change.** The team's code generator emits a conditional's arms and a function expression's result with no conversion (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`, `forIf` at `:3813` and `forFnExpr` at `:3423` in the team's last commit, `a874948ac`), and the team's class loader, to choose a call's opcode while it instantiates a template, loads and initializes the call's owner class (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:238` there). The tree casts a value of self's type at each arm of a conditional and at a function expression's or a local function's result, where the target type lies strictly below self's trait, and reads the owner's class file to choose the opcode, loading no class. So, compiled, a conditional with `self` in one arm and another value in the other runs at a type that self's trait's `comprises` clause lists and at the trait's self-type parameter (`compiler_tests/ComprisesValueAtConditionalArmRun`, `compiler_tests/SelfTypeArmRun`), as does a `case` expression's clause; a function expression or a local function that returns `self` there runs (`compiler_tests/ComprisesValueFromClosureRun`, `compiler_tests/SelfTypeFromClosureRun`); and a default body that calls a method on a value of the self-type parameter runs where the object lists the trait first (`compiler_tests/SelfTypeParameterReceiverRun`). A `typecase` with `self` in one arm and another value in the other still fails the JVM's verification when its class loads (`compiler_tests/XXXComprisesValueAtTypecaseArmRun`); its workaround stays: bind `self` at the target type in the arm. The reason: the specification types `self` as `T ∩ (U1 ∪ … ∪ Un)` under a `comprises` clause and as `T ∩ X` in the bodies of a trait with a self-type parameter `X` (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:64-80`), the checker accepts these bodies, and on the code before the change each failed when its class loaded: 'java.lang.VerifyError: Bad return type' for the arms and the closures, and 'java.lang.ClassCircularityError: …$Pt' for the default body. The skill's statement of the three failures and their workarounds (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:43-47`) holds no longer, but for the `typecase`.
132	
133	**Provenance.** Rows 1051, 1050 and 1052 (review-queue item 572); the batch record's forks Q1 (each arm and each closure's result cast where its static type is not already below the target, as a method's returned value is) and Q2 (the opcode chosen without loading a class that is being expanded), each taken at its default; P-146 and P-60; rung K of climb batch 31 for the cast; climb batch 33, rung Q. The `typecase` is row 1070, owed to the member of rung V.

136	
137	Revival change: none. The change brings the compiled path to what the specification says and walk does: a value of an intersection is a value of each conjunct (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:627-628`), a dotted call binds the receiver to the method's `self` (`Specification/basic/expressions/method-invocation.tex:47-48`), and walk runs the value's own method. The team's code generator narrowed an intersection receiver only where its conjuncts nest and crashed otherwise (`CodeGen.java:7420-7450`, `:7323` on the base), a failure that no source states as the language's behaviour; no rule of the language changes.

141	**The change.**

143	- The team's compiled checker reassociated a primary of several math items and left the result unchecked where every item applied to the front, writing the subscript as a subscript expression (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Operators.scala:310-320` and `:352-385` at 1609258002, the team's lines), so `x[5]^2` and `g[1][2]` did not compile. The tree accepts it: `compiler_tests/TopLevelVarByAssignExport.test`, `TopLevelVarByAssignImport.test`. Reason: `Specification/basic/variables.tex:85-95`, "The modifier var is optional when `:=` is used", and `Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:343`, which asks the same mutability.
145	- The team's checker left a local tuple binding's declared name unchecked beside untyped names (`Decls.scala`, the general `LocalVarDecl` case, the team's lines), so a mismatch compiled and a needed conversion did not happen. The tree converts or refuses: `compiler_tests/LocalTupleBindingMixedTypes.test`, `XXXLocalTupleBindingMixedRefused.test`. Reason: `Specification/basic/variables.tex:65` and `:195-198`; walk refuses the mismatch.
146	- The revival's numeral default (where nothing fixes a type) reaches a block's last expression after a local declaration or a local function: `compiler_tests/NumeralEndsUntypedBlockCompiled.test`. The team's compiler's prelude keeps a numeral's own type at such a place. Reason: `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:211-217`; the run's `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerBuiltin$v` before.

Declare the variable's type."; `references/tests-writing.md`, "`x[5]^2` stops the compile, and under walk fails or gives the wrong element (ledger rows 1005 and 1)" (now: compiles; fails under walk, row 1).

    Four of the compiled checker's smaller gaps repaired

#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
# The environment is env.sh's, set here without sourcing it, since env.sh also removes parser directories in
# /tmp. The tree is the one this script is in. FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is the pin of build.xml's fastTrack macro,
# which runs the gate's compiled tracks. The JVMs keep their temporary files, parser directories among them,
# in the tree's tmp/.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=4
mkdir -p "$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "${files[@]}" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
else
for t in "$@"; do
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit $t"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "$D/$t" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
done
fi
clean "$@"

content.content:
=== library-selector
## Sentences of the specification made false

None. Three sentences say that the compiled path compiles against its own library until the switch-over: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4608-4609`, `:5123-5124`, `:5384-5385`. They stay true: without the selection the compile command reads the prelude as before, and under it a program compiles against the one library but does not run, so the compiled path is not switched over.

Out of the specification, these statements of the record and the skill are now out of date; the gather corrects them:

- F-352, "on `main` the compile command selects the compiler's prelude alone", and F-353, "`main` has no selector and one set of classes" (`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md:170-171`).
- `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands": "Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude" (now: the one library's names under `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`).
- `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/build-and-caches.md`, "The caches" and "Building": the runs that read `default_repository/caches`, and the build's stamp over that folder (now also `default_repository/caches-one`).
- `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/tests-writing.md`, "Where a test goes, and how it passes": the compiled test folders are `library_tests/`, `parser_tests/`, `compiler_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/` (now also `one_library_tests/`, the compiled path against the one library, under the selection); and `tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests": "Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`" (now also `one_library_tests/`, whose files run in one JVM by `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one FORTRESS_CACHES=<folder> ../bin/fortress junit`, not by `junit.sh`, which cleans `default_repository/caches` by name).
- `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/tests-running.md`, "The two suites": `ant testFast` "runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks" (now a fifth, `onelibrary`, started when one of the four ends), and "One unit-test class, or one track" (now also `ant testOneLibrary`).

=== typecase-unbound-arm
=== kind-env-generic
## Sentences of the specification made false

None. `grep -rn "kind env\|row~812\|row~822" Specification/` finds nothing; Appendix I's sentence on such a trait (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1732-1734`, "The code generator compiles such a trait, but does not yet read a size off an argument at a call") stays true, and no sentence says that the code generator leaves a clause's names unbound.

=== self-arm-closure
## 7. Sentences of the specification made false

- `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4445-4449`, the effect of the entry on the self-type parameter: "A function expression or a local function that returns \KWD{self} as the self parameter still fails the JVM's verification when its class is loaded (row~1050 of the revival's gap ledger), and so does a default body that returns a conditional expression with \KWD{self} in one arm and another value of the self parameter in the other (row~1051)." Both now run (`SelfTypeFromClosureRun`, `SelfTypeArmRun`). The section does not have this rung edit it; the gather corrects it.
- No `\revision` or `\note` of `traits.tex` or `var-ref.tex` names these shapes.

Outside the specification, these say what the tree no longer does, for the gather and the skill writer: `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:43-47` (the three shapes and their workarounds); F-377 ("A closure's returned value and a conditional's arms get no cast (rows 1050 and 1051)") and F-225 (the shapes "that still fail verification", row 1051, and the `ClassCircularityError`, row 1052); the orientation key's case 35, (b) and (c) (`explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/regression/key.md:454-466`); and `PLAN.md:856`, the owed test, now written and promoted.

=== intersection-receiver
## 7. Sentences of the specification made false

- `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3740-3747`, the Effect of "The Meet Rule for traits with comprises clauses": "The compiled type checker departs from this in four ways: ...; its code generator stops at a method call on a value of such a type (row~540); ...". The clause is false now; the sentence then names three ways. The skeptic corrected it on the branch (SKEPTIC.md); it is `:3740-3746` now.

None other: `grep -rn '540' Specification --include=*.tex` finds only this place.

=== checker-small-gaps
## Sentences of the specification made false

None. The four repairs bring the compiled path to what `juxtameaning.tex`, `variables.tex`, `literals.tex` and `blocks.tex` say; no Appendix I Effect names rows 1005, 1028, 1029 or 1060 (`grep -n '1005\|1028\|1029\|1060' Specification/appendices/changes.tex` prints none). The Effect of the numerals' entry lists the implementations' departures from its text (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5466-5480`); row 1074 is a departure that the list does not name, for the gather.
