content.content:
# Writing a test

**gated test**
: Test that the gate's suites run.

**green**
: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as passed.

**red**
: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as failed.

**`XXX` test**
: Gated expected failure. It asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. The harness reports it green while it fails, and red when the defect is fixed.

## A test program

A test program has this form:

    component Name
    export Executable

    (* declarations *)

    run(): () = do
        assert(f(2), 4, "f(2)")
    end

    end

- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
- A compiled test with a `run` key ends `run()` with `println("PASS")`, unless a `run_out` key checks its output (below).
- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`. It and `=/=` call a type's own `=` only if the type extends a `FortressLibrary` trait that declares `=`, such as `Equality` (ledger row 807). Otherwise they compare by `SEQV` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). If a type `P` has its own `=`, make `P` extend `Equality[\P\]`, or write `assert(x = y, msg)`. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
- A superscript is `^` and what follows it, as the exponent in `x^2` or the transpose `^T`. It can follow a dotted access: `p.wq^T` is `(p.wq)^T`. After a call or a subscript, parenthesise first, as `(f(x))^T` and `(x[5])^2`: `f(x)^T` is a static error, and `x[5]^2` stops the compile, and under walk fails or gives the wrong element (ledger rows 1005 and 1).
- A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand, not a literal, because an expression of literals alone folds before the run (`revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").

## Where a test goes, and how it passes

Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.

- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test here records a refusal that walk misses: it is green while the program loads and runs clean, and red once walk refuses it.

Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:

- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series. Put no new test there.

The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:

    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)

A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. With `run_exits_nonzero=true`, the run must exit non-zero, as a program whose class fails to load does. The `run_*` checks, and the `PASS` check where no `run_out` check is given, still apply. For example:

    tests=EqualityRung1
    link
    run
    run_out_WIcontains=PASS

## How `XXX` works

- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.

## How a defect is recorded

Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:

1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.

If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. The change that next works there writes the test.

## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass

1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says.
3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.

The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.

In your report, quote two to five lines of the failing run, if there is one, and the passing line, each with its command. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A task that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key.

An edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` has no test. Check it as `specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", says.

## Writing an `XXX` test

In a compiled test folder, name the component `XXXName`, in its file `XXXName.fss` and in its `component` line.

- For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test, with `compile` and `compile_err_contains=<the refusal's message>`.
- For a code-generator wall (`compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet"), write `XXXName.test` with `tests=XXXName`, `compile` and `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`.
- For a program that compiles and fails at run time, write two `.test` files over the component:
  - `NameLink.test`, a plain name, with `tests=XXXName` and `link`. It is red if the link reports static errors, but green on an exception.
  - `XXXName.test`, with `tests=XXXName` and `run`, and no `link`. Its run uses the plain file's link, so run the two files in one call of `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`, the plain one first.
  - The program prints `REACHED` in `run()` before the part that fails. The `XXX` file checks it with `run_out_contains=REACHED`, or with `run_out_does_not_contain=REACHED` if the run dies before `run()` prints. Never use `run_out_contains=PASS`.
  - Example: `compiler_tests/XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW.test` and `BoxDotSpellingsRungWLink.test`.

Show the first `XXX` test that your change adds, and only the first, working through the harness (`harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`), from its place in a gated test folder. Run it twice:

1. As it is: the harness must report an expected failure.
2. Changed for one run so that the defect does not show, then restored: the harness must report it red. For example, add the missing declaration to the test program, set the expected string to what the run prints, or, in a run-time pair, remove the part that fails.

## Promoting an `XXX` test

If your change fixes a defect that has a gated `XXX` test, the fix turns that test red. To find such a test, search the gap ledger (`records.md`): a row's reproducer names it. Also list the `XXX` files: `git ls-files 'ProjectFortress/*XXX*'`. Then promote it:

1. Before you edit the code, remove the prefix: give the test a plain name by its topic. Rename each file with `git mv` (`committing.md` gives the commit), or with `mv` if the file is not committed yet. 2. See the plain-named test fail through the harness on the base's code, as "The order", step 2, says.
3. Make the fix and see the test pass.

A run-time pair keeps its three files, renamed without `XXX`. For example, `compiler_tests/NatRtTask` was promoted so in `fd5cb4864`:

- `Name.fss`, with `component Name`. The program asserts its values, then prints `PASS` last.
- `NameLink.test`: `tests=Name` and `link`.
- `Name.test`, in place of `XXXName.test`: `tests=Name`, `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`.

- Name a test by its topic. Give it one comment line that says what it checks, with no pointer to a record.
- Assert each case in one test only. Add a new case to the test that already asserts cases of its kind: `git grep` for the case's name or value finds it. A case that fails today goes in an `XXX` test, since it would turn a plain test red.
- Write an assertion's message as one short line that says what was checked. Put a reason that several assertions share in one comment line above them.
- In a test, cite the specification by file and section or entry, never by line: `opr-overview.tex, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators"`. In the library chapters, name the entry too: `basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", opr CHOOSE`.

For one thread, run the program directly with the prefix `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (a compiled program: `compiler.md`, "Running"), and check its exit code and output.

(* A subscript followed by a superscript, another subscript or a tightly juxtaposed item applies each in turn, left to right (juxtameaning.tex, section "Juxtaposition"). *)
component SubscriptThenSuperscriptCompiled
export Executable

object Mat(v: ZZ32)
    opr [i: ZZ32]: ZZ32 = v + i
end

object Grid(v: ZZ32)
    opr [i: ZZ32]: Mat = Mat(v + i)
end

mk(): Mat = Mat(1)

object Maker
    f(): Mat = Mat(2)
end

run(): () = do
    x = Mat(7)
    assert(x[5]^2, 144, "x[5]^2")
    y: ZZ32 = x[2]^3
    assert(y, 729, "x[2]^3 at a declared type")
    assert((mk())[5]^2, 36, "(mk())[5]^2")
    assert(Maker.f()[5]^2, 49, "Maker.f()[5]^2")
    g = Grid(7)
    assert(g[1][2], 10, "g[1][2]")
    assert(g[1][2]^2, 100, "g[1][2]^2")
    k: ZZ32 = 3
    assert(x[5]k, 36, "x[5]k")
    println("PASS")
end

end
tests=SubscriptThenSuperscriptCompiled
link
run
run_out_contains=PASS

content.content:
- F-363 **A superscript follows a dotted access and a parenthesised call on both paths.** `p.wq^T`, `B.n^2`, `B.f()^T` and `B.data[5]^2` parse as the operator applied to the whole dotted primary to its left, and `(f(x))^T`, `(f(x))!` and `(a^b)!` run under walk as they do compiled; `f(x)^T` and `f(x)^2` stay a static error on both paths (walk: "the argument should not be immediately followed by a non-expression element"; the checker: "Item at this location must be an expression, not an operator."). The parser reads a primary with a dot as the front of the math items that follow it (`parser/Expression.rats:386-400`), so a subscript, a parenthesised item or a tight identifier after a dotted method call parses too, which no test asserts; the one node kind it builds for a single item is the one the parenthesised spelling built, so neither the checker nor the code generator changed. Walk's postfix branch evaluates an operand in parentheses as one expression (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:965-970`). So a model line may write `p.wq^T x` and `(onehot(ks, 5))^T dx`; a selector after a superscript, `B.data^T.v`, is still a syntax error, and a superscript after a subscript that is a math item of its own, `x[5]^2` or `B.f()[5]^2`, still fails on both paths (row 1 under walk, row 1005 compiled); in `B.data[5]^2` the subscript is part of the dotted primary. Tests: `tests/SuperscriptAfterDottedAccess.fss`, `tests/SuperscriptAfterParenthesisedCall.fss`, `tests/SuperscriptAfterCallRefused.fss` with its `.test`, and `compiler_tests/SuperscriptAfterDottedAccessCompiled.test`, `SuperscriptAfterParenthesisedCallCompiled.test`, `XXXSuperscriptAfterCallRefusedCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-superscript-after/REPORT.md`, "Each form on the base and after" and "The trees".
16:2. **Row 1005, a subscript followed by a superscript** (commit d7ec58bdf3). The parser builds a `MathPrimary` of two or more math items for `x[5]^2`, and the checker reassociates it (`Operators.scala`, `checkExprOperators`, case `SMathPrimary`). Where every item applied in turn to the front, the reassociation left one application and no element after it; the checker then tried a juxtaposition of that one element, which no declaration takes, and returned the application unchecked, so the compile stopped: 'Result of typechecking still contains intermediate nodes.' #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'

- **Trap.** A built-in number type is an abstract type with a concrete run-time object below it. A program then names that object in a `typecase`, a type or a test, and a program's own type extends the number type to take its operators, as a Haskell type joins `Num`. Its sources (climb batch 31b's `orientation/admission.md`, F-379's row):
  - the specification's `trait ℤ` (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:229`);
  - the team's library, which declared `trait ZZ32 … comprises { Int, IntLiteral }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`, and `Float`, `Long`, `UnsignedLong` and `BigNum` in the same way (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss:642`, and `trait RR64 … comprises { Float, FloatLiteral, RR32, QQ }` at `:422`; `a874948ac:ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:369`, `Int`, and `:54`, `Float`; climb batch 31b's `RECORD.md`, rung O's revival change);
  - the team's `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss`, whose `typecase` had arms at `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` until rung O respelled them (`f6e24650e7`);
  - the skill's area parts, which still name the five as current (`interpreter.md:121`, `:127`, and `:141`, where a program's object that extends `ZZ32` loads; `compiler.md:22`, `:99`; `library.md:39`), as this key's case 29 did until this update;
  - the audit's proposed core line "Numbers are library traits, side by side" (`skills-distillation-audit.md:364`).

  Worker failures. After `IntLiteral` left the one library, `tests/IntegerConversionsWalk.fss`'s `shown` printed '-2147483648 : IntLiteral' for a `ZZ32`, until its arms were removed (row 959's note). Before climb batch 27, 48 lines of revival tests asserted printed `Int` names (case 29's **Trap**). Rung O's skeptic ran the arms `Int`, `Float` and `else` on `3`, `1.5` and `"s"`: the base answered `3 Int; 1.5 Float; s else`, and the landed tree `3 Int; 1.5 Int; s Int`, "the one landed change that turns a right answer into a silent wrong one for a program that still names `Int`" (`reviews/batch-31b-review.md`, section 2, O4). For the extender: on the base, `object Mine extends ZZ32` loaded unde
- **Expected.**
  - (a) Neither assertion runs: walk refuses the program at load, 'Int is undefined.' at the arm `Int` and 'Float is undefined.' at `Float`. No library declares `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` or `UnsignedLong` since climb batch 31b (P-178, F-379), and a `typecase` arm at a name that no declaration defines is refused where names are bound, on both paths, as every other undefined type name is (F-382; row 959, fixed by climb batch 33's rung D).
  - (b) Arms at the library's own names: `ZZ32` in place of `Int` and `RR64` in place of `Float`, with `else`; `ZZ64`, `ZZ` and `NN64` stand in place of `Long`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong`. At `kind`'s `Number` parameter the numerals take their defaults, `ZZ32` for `3` and `RR64` for `1.5` (P-173). So the assertions are that `kind(3)` is "ZZ32" and `kind(1.5)` is "RR64". The strings are the test's own: "Int" and "Float" kept as the labels of arms at `ZZ32` and `RR64` are right too. `Meters` goes below `Number`, with its own operators:

        value object Meters(v: ZZ32) extends Number
          opr +(self, other: Meters): Meters = Meters(v + other.v)
        end

    It needs `Number` as a parent to be passed to `kind`. Without it, walk stops at the call, 'Unification error: Closure/Constructor for kind param 1 (x:Number) got arg Meters of type Meters'. `kind(Meters(2))` gives "other", or the label of an arm at `Meters` if the reader adds one. An assertion such as `(Meters(2) + Meters(3)).v` = 5 checks the `+`. A plain `object` in place of `value object` is right too.
  - (c) The planned `object Meters(v: ZZ32) extends ZZ32`: walk refuses the program at load, 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'. `ZZ32` is one value object, an object is a leaf, and no type of a program extends a built-in number type (P-178, F-379; `tests/NumberTypeExtendRefusedWalk.fss`). On the compiled path today the checker accepts it, since the compiler's prelude still declares `ZZ32` an open trait (row 1003). The run then dies when the object's class loads, before `run()` prints anything: 'IncompatibleClassChangeError: class …$Meters can not implement com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32, because it is not an interface' (row 866). The reader's `Meters` below `Number` loads
- **Scope.** The arms behave alike on both paths. The team's arms are refused on both paths, 'Int is undefined.', at load under walk and by the compile (F-382), and the repaired arms compile and run. The extender differs by path today: refused at load under walk, dead at class load when compiled. This holds until the prelude takes P-178's form (decided and not built: review-queue item 577, fork H2) or until the switch-over (row 866, "Ends when"). Other points, none needed for a right answer:
  - A trait of the program's own below `ZZ32` is refused at load under walk too, with the same message (this update's probe; the record has no run of it).
  - A removed name as a type is refused at load: `describe(x: Int)` stops, 'Int is undefined.' (this update's probe; F-303 for `Float`).
  - A trait of the program's own below `Number` that declares its own functional `+` fails the Meet Rule beside the library's `+` between an array and a number, unless it excludes the arrays (case 27; P-160, row 918). An object such as `Meters` does not (case 12).
  - Row 959's fix, climb batch 33's rung D, refuses such an arm at load, as `tests/TypecaseUndefinedArmWalk.test` asserts ('NoSuchTypeHere is undefined'). An element of a tuple of names, as `(x, y) =>`, still binds (row 1064).
- **Wrong.**
  - (a) "Int" and "Float", as the arms read; "Int" for both values, the first arm taking every value, as before row 959's fix; either assertion said to run.
  - (b) An arm, a type, a test or a message at `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` or `UnsignedLong`, on either path. `Meters` below `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `RR64`, or below a trait of the program's own that extends one. `Meters` with no `Number` parent, passed to `kind`.
  - (c) The planned declaration said to load under walk, to be refused by the compiled checker today, or to compile and run; walk's refusal reported as a defect.
- **Partial.**
  - (a) and (b) right, with no compiled answer in (c), or with the compiled extender said to be refused as it is under walk.
  - (b) right, with no word on why `extends ZZ32` cannot stand.
  - (a) with the refusal at load, but without the name that it gives.
- **Open.** P-178 has the compiler's prelude take the same form before the switch-over, and the way is review-queue item 577 (fork H2; default: a probe of way (a), then one rung). No run shows what the compiled path then does with the extender: a static refusal or another failure. The question asks about today, so a right answer does not need it. Whether walk's refusal covers `QQ`, the number type that stays a trait, is not settled either (climb batch 31b's `orientation/preserve.md`, failure 2). The question does not reach it.
- **Skill.**
  - The orientation, "Numbers", as climb batch 31b's update words it: the rule "The number types are flat siblings (P-43)", with its sentences on the seven value objects, the refusal at load and the prelude's open traits (rows 1003 and 866); the rule "The team's `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` do not exist", with the `typecase` arm (row 959) and the five names to write in their place; and the rule "A numeral converts where it stands", for the defaults at `Number`.
  - The core: "Numbers are siblings, not a tower" and "Traits and objects, no classes" (an object is a leaf).
  - Stale beside these: `interpreter.md:121` and `:127` ("Natives"), `:141` (a program's object that extends `ZZ32` loads), `compiler.md:22` and `:99`, and `library.md:39` (climb batch 31b's `orientation/admission.md`, "Outside the orientation"). A reader misled there fails the case against that area part, not against the orientation.
  - The orientation before this update (`revival-changes.md` at `e64da5d944`, `:95` and `:116`) says only that the types are flat siblings and that a program may declare its own number type below `Number`. It is the baseline without the candidate.
- **Evidence.** P-178, P-160, P-166, P-43, P-173; F-379, F-303, F-344; rows 959, 1003, 866 and 551; review-queue items 519 and 577. The tests: `tests/NumberTypeExtendRefusedWalk.fss` with its `.test` ('Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'), `tests/NumberTypesAreObjectsWalk.fss`, `tests/XXXTypecaseUndefinedArmWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/XXXObjectExtendsZZ32Compiled.fss`. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-library-selector/REPORT.md:225`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/repository/ProjectProperties.java:290-291`, `bin/run_classpath:27-31`.

Against: the team built and tested the form, and the chapter defers patterns to the pattern-matching proposal. Default: as landed, the form kept and the row open. Should the specification state the form? If the chapter is held silent on them, as row 498 has it, row 1068's expected-failure walk test, which reads `typecase.tex:93-94` and `:107-109` as binding each name to its element, becomes a row alone. No default on record; as landed, the test kept. s do not depend on the JVM's identity hashes, except at inference variables, walk's wrapped values and the nodes that hold them.** Every generated node's hash starts from the hash of its class's name: makeAST's post-processing of ASTGen's output writes that start, and so do the in-repo generators (`build.xml:679-697`). A field whose type holds an `Option` is hashed
    <!-- Hash each node apart from the JVM's identity hashes, so that hash
         maps and sets of nodes iterate in one order whatever code asked for
         an identity hash before.  ASTGen's NodeClass starts each node's
         hash from the Class object's identity hash: start it from the hash
         of the class's name, which String.hashCode fixes.  The Option
         classes hash by identity hashes too, so a field whose type holds an
         Option is hashed by NodeHash.  The in-repo generators write the
         class name's hash directly, and none of their fields holds an
         Option. -->
    <replaceregexp byline="true"
                   match="^(\s*int code = getClass\(\))\.hashCode\(\);$"
                   replace="\1.getName().hashCode();">
      <fileset dir="${nodes}" includes="**/*.java"/>
    </replaceregexp>
    <replaceregexp flags="g"
                   match="(Option<[^\n]*> (temp_\w+) = [^\n]*;\n\s*code \^= )\2\.hashCode\(\);"
                   replace="\1NodeHash.of(\2);">
      <fileset dir="${nodes}" includes="**/*.java"/>
    </replaceregexp>

(* A typecase clause's name, alone or in a tuple pattern, bound at a trait above its selector's object type, takes a method call as the object it is, compiled (typecase.tex, section "Typecase Expressions": its static type is the intersection of the two). *)
component XXXTypecaseClauseNameAboveSelector
export Executable

trait Shape
  nm(): String
end
object Sq extends Shape
  nm(): String = "sq"
end

object Probe
  viaOne(a: Sq): String =
    typecase a of
      x: Shape => x.nm()
      else => "else"
    end
  viaPair(a: Sq, b: Any): String =
    typecase (a, b) of
      (x: Shape, n: ZZ32) => x.nm() || n.asString
      else => "else"
    end
end

run(): () = do
  println("REACHED")
  assert(Probe.viaOne(Sq), "sq", "a clause's name at a trait above the selector's object type")
  assert(Probe.viaPair(Sq, 1), "sq1", "a tuple pattern's name at a trait above its element's object type")
  println("PASS")
end

end
(* Under walk, a name of a typecase clause's tuple pattern beside an element given by its type alone is bound to its own element, not to the whole tuple (typecase.tex, section "Typecase Expressions"). *)
component XXXTypecaseTypeOnlyElementWalk
export Executable

tag(x: String): String = "string " || x

first(a: Any, b: Any): String =
  typecase (a, b) of
    (s: String, ZZ32) => tag(s)
    else => "other"
  end

second(a: Any, b: Any): String =
  typecase (a, b) of
    (ZZ32, s: String) => tag(s)
    else => "other"
  end

run(): () = do
  assert(first("m", 1), "string m", "the name before a type-only element")
  assert(second(2, "n"), "string n", "the name after a type-only element")
end

end

\item If there is any non-expression element (it cannot be the first element)
then replace the first such element and the element immediately preceding it
(which must be an expression) with a single element that does the appropriate
operator application.  This new element is an expression.  Reassociate the
resulting sequence (which is one element shorter).
\item Otherwise, the sequence necessarily has only expression elements,
only the last of which may be a function.

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
